name: Validating AI in GxP Systems
blurb: GAMP, computer software assurance and risk based validation for AI.
title: Validating AI in GxP Systems
answer: Validation of AI builds on existing practice rather than replacing it. ISPE's GAMP guide on artificial intelligence extends GAMP 5 to AI, and the FDA's computer software assurance guidance moves validation toward risk based testing focused on what matters for product quality. The hard parts specific to AI are proving the training data is fit, testing on independent data and controlling model changes.

reading.body:
Validating AI in GxP systems extends existing GAMP and computer software assurance practice rather than replacing it, with the hard parts being training data fitness, independent testing, and model change control.

The pattern is continuity. ISPE's GAMP guide on artificial intelligence extends GAMP 5 and its data integrity guidance to AI systems, and the FDA's computer software assurance guidance, finalized in September 2025, moves validation toward risk based testing focused on what matters for product quality. Neither framework invents a separate regime for AI. The FDA's Quality Management System Regulation, effective February 2026 for device makers, sits alongside them as the quality system context these validations run inside.

For AI specifically, the difficulty is not the paperwork but three properties of models. Training data must be shown fit for purpose, which is a data provenance and integrity problem before it is a model problem. Testing must run on data the model never saw in training, which breaks the habit of validating a system against the same inputs it was built on. And every model change must fall under change control, which is awkward when retraining can alter behavior without any change to the surrounding software.

The data does not say how regulators will treat specific model architectures, what evidence thresholds will satisfy reviewers in practice, or how validation burden scales with model size. It covers guidance and effective dates, not enforcement outcomes.

explainer:
Computerised system validation proves that a system does what it is supposed to do, consistently, in its intended use. The industry's reference approach is GAMP 5, which scales effort to risk and to how complex or customised a system is. The FDA's computer software assurance guidance pushes in the same direction, asking companies to focus testing on functions that could affect product quality or patient safety and to use lighter, unscripted testing elsewhere.

AI adds problems traditional validation did not face. Performance depends on training data, so the data must be shown fit for purpose and representative. Testing must use data the model never saw, and acceptance criteria must be fixed beforehand to avoid tuning to the test. Behaviour can shift as real world inputs drift, so monitoring after go-live matters more than for conventional software. And models are retrained, so change control must cover data and model versions, not just code. ISPE's GAMP guide on AI brings these points into the existing framework rather than creating a separate one.

The parts that carry over

GxP validation has a settled shape: user requirements, risk assessment, supplier assessment, installation and operational qualification, performance qualification against the intended use, and change control for the system's life. All of that still applies to an AI system. What changes is the content of each part, because the thing being validated is a model whose behaviour comes from data rather than a procedure that can be read.

The parts that change

User requirements have to state the model's intended use, the input range it is built for and the performance it must achieve, including on rare and difficult cases. Risk assessment has to consider failure modes that ordinary software does not have: drift as inputs change, bias across subgroups, confident wrong outputs, and silent changes from retraining or vendor updates. Performance qualification needs test data independent of training data, representative of real operation and locked before testing, with results reported across subgroups. Operation adds performance monitoring with thresholds that trigger review. And change control treats every retraining and every model version as a change needing its own evidence.

The common mistakes

Testing on data the model was trained on, which proves nothing. Validating once and never monitoring, so drift goes unseen. Accepting a vendor's validation package without checking it reflects the company's own data and use. Letting a vendor update a model without the company knowing. And writing human oversight into the procedure without designing it into the system, so the review becomes a formality. Avoiding those five covers most of what inspectors have found wrong with AI validation so far.
